newsitem.title: UK: West more confident about Yeltsin this time around.
newsitem.headline: West more confident about Yeltsin this time around.

text.p: The West has learned to live with Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health problems, with only muted foreign reaction to his latest illness and widespread confidence that he remains in charge and on track for recovery.

Diplomats say there is less uncertainty surrounding Yeltsin's authority -- as well as his health -- this time, compared with the turmoil which preceded his major heart surgery just over two months ago.
The Kremlin has said Yeltsin, 65, is in hospital with pneumonia.

Financial markets and even the Russian people, used to being deceived about the health of their leaders over the years, seem to believe the authorities this time and the same is true for Western governments.

"We have no reason to think Yeltsin will not be returning to work, which is what worried us last year," said one Western envoy. "There is also more confidence in the stability of Russian politics now, far more than when he had the bypass."
Nevertheless, Yeltsin's illness comes at a difficult time in relations with the West.
Moscow remains deeply opposed to NATO's plans for enlargement, which will take a major step forward in July when several Eastern European countries will be invited to join.

Diplomats said Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, respected as a skilled operator by Washington and its European allies, would handle most of the sensitive negotiations between Russia and the Western alliance.
There had been some question about whether Yeltsin was ready to take an easier line towards NATO now that enlargement is going ahead.
But it became clear when German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met Yeltsin last weekend that the Russian leader is taking a hard line and demanding concessions from the West.

"We are now sure that it will be a rough ride in the months ahead with the Russians, and that is Yeltsin's decision. Primakov and the others involved will have no trouble carrying that forward for him if he is ill," said another diplomat.
Russian television has reported that Yeltsin is in contact with a number of foreign leaders -- none of whom have expressed major concern about Yeltsin's health this time around.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has sent a "get well soon" message to Yeltsin and Germany's Kohl has said he sees no reason why Yeltsin should step down for health reasons.
Before Yeltsin's heart surgery, there was Western concern about power struggles in the Kremlin and the possibility of a major crisis in the Russian leader's absence.

In the end, Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin showed he had a firm grip on the reins of power and the threat of a crisis passed -- two additional factors which diplomats say have given the West more confidence this time around.
Chernomyrdin himself displayed similar confidence by starting a planned holiday near Moscow this week.

General Alexander Lebed, a popular figure in Russia even though he was sacked as national security adviser last year, has called on Yeltsin to quit and says the country is without leadership at a crucial time.
Western diplomats have largely discounted this as political manoeuvring. "You would expect Lebed to say that," said another envoy. "We believe things are better this time, not worse."
